title: Attend to your own soul
hookLine: no one is unhappy for ignoring another's mind, only their own (Meditations 2.8)

lines: FINE. AND A LOOK AT THE TABLE.
cards: A colleague says fine in the meeting, and nothing else. Not fine, let's do it. Just fine, and a look at the table.
What did that mean? Is he annoyed? Was it something said last week?
A question like that can follow a person home and sit with them at dinner. In book two, Marcus makes a blunt observation about where that attention would be better spent.

teach.h: NOT KNOWING THEIR MIND: SELDOM MISERY.
teach.b: First, the line. Section eight is two sentences. Hardly anyone, Marcus says, has been seen to be unhappy because they didn't notice what was going on in someone else's mind.
But people who don't follow the movements of their own minds are bound to be unhappy. Second, the honest word. He doesn't say never.
He says hardly anyone, or seldom. Sometimes misreading someone does cost something, and Marcus isn't pretending otherwise. He's pointing at which kind of attention pays.
Third, the movements of the mind.
For the Stoics, the mind is always moving.
An impression arrives: he's annoyed with me. Then comes a moment when you agree to it, or don't. Then an impulse: send a worried text, go cold, rehearse an argument.

Catching the impression before you agree to it is the heart of the practice. Epictetus said it in the handbook that opened this year: test the impression first. Marcus writes the same lesson to himself.
Fourth, where to point the flashlight.

You can't see into his mind, however long you replay the word fine. You can see into your own: the story you're telling, the fear under it, the reaction you're about to have. That's the one mind you can actually tend.
This isn't selfishness. Elsewhere in this same book, Marcus says people were made to work together, like hands or feet. Attending to your own soul is what makes you safe to be around.

how: Some people practicing Stoicism do brief check-ins during the day, noticing their own impressions and reactions instead of trying to decode what others are thinking.

games.q: what does “attend to your own soul” mean?
o: guess what others think, so you can avoid conflict
keep your private thoughts hidden from everyone
watch the movements of your own mind, not others'

games.q: attend to your own soul — tap the pairs.

s: Marcus says misreading other people never causes trouble
he says hardly anyone, seldom; the trouble he warns about is not watching your own mind.
Marcus says those who don't watch their own minds are bound to be unhappy
attending to your own soul means not caring about others
in the same book Marcus says we were made to work together.

games.q: a friend replies 'okay.' with a period. you feel the worry start. what fits Meditations 2.8?
o: analyze the message with three friends.
notice the story you're telling yourself, and tend that.
games.why: you can't see into her mind; you can watch the movements of your own. that's where Marcus points.

practice: Check in the way Marcus suggests: what's moving in your mind right now, a worry, a plan, a replay of a conversation? Name it quietly, then ask whether it's about your own mind or a guess at someone else's.
If it's a guess, gently bring the flashlight back to what you're feeling underneath.

wordCard.voice: Attend to your own soul. Few are made unhappy by not reading another's mind; those who don't watch their own are bound to be. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: soul, life, mind. Marcus watches the 'movements' of his own.

carryVoice: Your line: mind my own mind. The flashlight works best when it's pointed inward. Until tomorrow.
